**Cyanocobalamin** is the chemical name of **vitamin B₁₂** ✓ — the name itself describes the
molecule: a **cyano** group attached to a **cobalt** atom held in a **corrin** ring.
It is the only vitamin that contains a **metal atom**, and the cobalt at its centre is what
makes the crystals a deep red. It is also the largest and most complex of the vitamins.
Its roles: the formation of **red blood cells** and the maintenance of the nervous system.
Deficiency causes **pernicious anaemia**, with the production of abnormally large, immature
red cells, and in prolonged cases nerve damage.
Two features make it unusual as a dietary requirement. It is found almost exclusively in
**animal sources** — meat, liver, eggs, dairy — so strict vegetarians and vegans need a
supplement. And its absorption requires a protein secreted by the stomach called **intrinsic
factor**; where that is absent, anaemia follows however much B₁₂ is eaten, which is the
classic cause of pernicious anaemia.
The other B vitamins named in the options have quite different chemical names:
**(a) B₁** is **thiamine**, **(b) B₂** is **riboflavin**, **(c) B₆** is **pyridoxine**
(and the 'β₁' in option (a) is a misprint for B₁).
∴ Vitamin B₁₂.

**Vitamin A is retinol** ✓ — a fat-soluble alcohol with a long conjugated chain of double
bonds ending in a ring, found in fish-liver oils, milk, butter and eggs.
In the body it is oxidised to **retinal**, the aldehyde, which combines with the protein
opsin to form **rhodopsin**, the light-sensitive pigment of the retina. When light strikes
rhodopsin the retinal changes from the *cis* to the *trans* shape, and that single geometric
change is what triggers the nerve impulse we see by.
Deficiency therefore shows first as **night blindness** — too little rhodopsin to work in dim
light — and in prolonged cases as **xerophthalmia**, drying and ulceration of the cornea.
Plants supply it indirectly as **β-carotene**, the orange pigment of carrots, which the body
splits into two molecules of retinol.
The other names in the options belong to other vitamins, and knowing them settles the
question at once:
**(a) ascorbic acid** = vitamin **C** (deficiency: scurvy)
**(c) calciferol** = vitamin **D** (deficiency: rickets)
**(d) thiamine** = vitamin **B₁** (deficiency: beri-beri)
∴ retinol.

**Vitamin E** is the antisterility vitamin ✓ — chemically **tocopherol**, a name coined from
the Greek *tokos*, childbirth, and *pherein*, to carry, with the *-ol* ending for an alcohol.
The name was given because rats deprived of it became **infertile**, and the deficiency in
humans is associated with reproductive problems as well as muscular weakness.
It is a **fat-soluble** vitamin, found in vegetable oils (wheat germ, sunflower, cottonseed),
nuts and green leafy vegetables. Its chemical role is as an **antioxidant**: it mops up free
radicals and so protects the unsaturated lipids of cell membranes from oxidation, which is
also why it is added to oils and fats to stop them going rancid.
Deficiency is rare in humans, since the vitamin is widespread in the diet and stored in
fatty tissue.
The other options have well-known deficiency diseases of their own, none of them to do with
fertility:
**(a) vitamin D** — rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults
**(b) the B group** — beri-beri, pellagra, cheilosis, pernicious anaemia
**(d) vitamin A** — night blindness and xerophthalmia
∴ vitamin E.

A **nucleotide** has **three** components: a nitrogenous **base**, a pentose **sugar** and a
**phosphate** group ✓ — option (d).
The distinction worth fixing firmly is between the two related terms:
**Nucleoside** = **base + sugar** (two parts)
**Nucleotide** = **base + sugar + phosphate** (three parts)
So a nucleotide is a nucleoside that has been **phosphorylated**. The names help: *nucleoTide*
has the extra syllable, and the extra component.
How they are joined:
the base attaches to **C-1′** of the sugar, through a nitrogen, by a glycosidic bond
the phosphate esterifies the **C-5′** hydroxyl
The sugar is **ribose** in RNA and **2′-deoxyribose** in DNA, and the base is one of adenine,
guanine, cytosine, thymine (DNA) or uracil (RNA).
Nucleotides are the **monomers of nucleic acids**: a chain is built by phosphodiester bonds
linking the 5′-phosphate of one to the 3′-hydroxyl of the next.
They matter outside nucleic acids too — **ATP**, the cell's energy currency, is simply the
nucleotide adenosine with three phosphates instead of one.
Options (a), (b) and (c) each leave one of the three components out.
∴ base + sugar + phosphate.

**(a) Both are polymers of nucleotides** ✓ **correct.** DNA and RNA are each a long chain of
nucleotide units joined by **phosphodiester** bonds, running from the 5′-phosphate of one
sugar to the 3′-hydroxyl of the next. That shared backbone chemistry is their fundamental
similarity.

record: **ribose** in RNA, **2′-deoxyribose** in DNA — the latter lacking the hydroxyl at
C-2′. That missing oxygen makes DNA chemically more stable, which suits its role as the
permanent store of information.
**(d) 'similar type of pyrimidine bases'** ✗ Both contain **cytosine**, but the second
pyrimidine differs: **thymine** in DNA, **uracil** in RNA. (The purines, adenine and guanine,
are the same in both — so the statement is half true, which is what makes it tempting.)

**purines** — **adenine** and **guanine**, in **both** DNA and RNA
**pyrimidines** — **cytosine** in both, then **thymine in DNA** and **uracil in RNA**
So the base present in DNA but not in RNA is **thymine** ✓ — option (d).
(a) cytosine, (b) guanine and (c) adenine all occur in both, so none of them can be the
answer.
Thymine and uracil are in fact nearly the same molecule: **thymine is 5-methyluracil**, uracil
with one extra methyl group. That single methyl is worth a word, because it is not
decorative. Cytosine spontaneously deaminates to uracil at a slow but steady rate; if uracil
were a normal DNA base, the repair machinery could not tell such damage from legitimate
sequence. Because DNA uses **thymine** instead, any uracil found in DNA is recognised at once
as damage and excised — a small chemical difference that protects the integrity of the
genetic record.
RNA, being short-lived and continually remade, has no such need and uses the cheaper uracil.
The complementary question — which base is in RNA but not DNA — has the answer **uracil**.

Nucleotides are joined into a chain by a **phosphodiester** linkage, and the question is which
carbons of the sugar it connects.
A phosphate group sits on the **5′-carbon** of one nucleotide. It forms a second ester bond
to the **3′-hydroxyl** of the next sugar, so the bridge runs
**C-5′ of one sugar — O — P — O — C-3′ of the next**
Hence the linkage is between the **5′ and 3′** carbons ✓ — option (a).
It is called a **di**ester because the single phosphorus atom is esterified **twice**, once to
each sugar.
This 5′→3′ connection is what gives a nucleic acid strand its **direction**. One end of the
chain has a free 5′-phosphate and the other a free 3′-hydroxyl, so the two ends are
chemically different, and sequences are always written 5′ to 3′. DNA polymerase can add
nucleotides only at the **3′ end**, which is why replication runs in one direction and why
the lagging strand must be made in fragments.
Why the other carbons are not involved: **C-1′** carries the nitrogenous **base**, and C-2′
carries the hydroxyl that distinguishes ribose from deoxyribose — neither is available for
the backbone.
∴ 5′ and 3′.

The **α-helix** is a form of **secondary** structure, and secondary structure is held together
by **hydrogen bonds** ✓.
The bonds form along the **backbone** of the chain, not between side chains:
the **>C=O** of one peptide link is the acceptor
the **>N–H** of a peptide link further along is the donor
In the α-helix specifically, the bond runs from the C=O of residue *n* to the N–H of residue
**n + 4**. That spacing is what fixes the geometry of the helix — **3·6 residues per turn**,
a pitch of 5·4 Å, and a right-handed twist — with all the side chains projecting outwards.
Why the others are wrong:
**(a) Peptide bonds** ✗ These are the **covalent** C–N links joining the amino acids. They
constitute the **primary** structure; they make the chain but do not fold it. This is the
most tempting distractor precisely because peptide bonds are so central.
**(b) van der Waals forces** and **(d) dipole-dipole interactions** ✗ Both are present but far
too weak to impose a regular repeating structure.
A single hydrogen bond is worth only about 20 kJ mol⁻¹, but a helix of a hundred residues has
nearly a hundred of them acting together, and that is what makes the arrangement stable.
Breaking them — by heat, acid or urea — is exactly what **denaturation** is: the helix
unwinds and the protein stops working.
∴ hydrogen bonds.

These are the four **tetroses** (aldoses with four carbons). Each has two chiral centres,
C-2 and C-3, so there are 2² = 4 stereoisomers: D- and L-erythrose and D- and L-threose.
Two rules identify each structure in a **Fischer projection** drawn with CHO at the top:
**D or L** — look at the **penultimate** chiral carbon, here **C-3**, the lower one.
OH on the **right** ⟹ **D**; OH on the **left** ⟹ **L**
**erythro or threo** — look at whether the two hydroxyls are on the **same** side.
same side ⟹ **erythrose**; opposite sides ⟹ **threose**
Now read the four structures from left to right:
**1st** — C-2 OH right, C-3 OH **right** ⟹ D; both on the same side ⟹ erythrose ⟹
**D-erythrose**
**2nd** — C-2 OH left, C-3 OH **right** ⟹ D; opposite sides ⟹ threose ⟹ **D-threose**
**3rd** — C-2 OH left, C-3 OH **left** ⟹ L; same side ⟹ erythrose ⟹ **L-erythrose**
**4th** — C-2 OH right, C-3 OH **left** ⟹ L; opposite sides ⟹ threose ⟹ **L-threose**
So the order is **D-erythrose, D-threose, L-erythrose, L-threose** ✓
Notice the 1st and 3rd are mirror images, as are the 2nd and 4th — each pair is a set of
**enantiomers**, while any D–L mixed pair across the two names are **diastereomers**.
∴ D-erythrose, D-threose, L-erythrose, L-threose.

the **anomeric** carbon formed when the open chain closes into a ring. Stereoisomers related
in exactly that way are called **anomers** ✓.
In the pyranose ring, the C-1 hydroxyl points **down** in the α form and **up** in the β form;
every other centre is identical.

**(a) Enantiomers** ✗ — non-superimposable mirror images, which would require **every** chiral
centre to be inverted. Here only one is, so the two are **diastereomers**, not enantiomers.
(The enantiomer of α-D-glucose is α-L-glucose.)
**(c) Epimers** ✗ — this is close but not exact. Epimers differ at **one** chiral centre, which
is true here; but when that centre is specifically the **anomeric** carbon of a cyclic sugar,
the pair gets the more precise name **anomers**. Anomers are a special case of epimers, so
the better answer is (d). (Glucose and galactose, differing at C-4, are epimers but not
anomers.)

cannot, because a bond must be broken to change the configuration at C-1.
The two really are distinct substances: α melts at 146 °C with [α] = +111°, β at 150 °C with
[α] = +19°. In water each slowly converts to an equilibrium mixture, which is
**mutarotation**.

Sucrose is built from **glucose and fructose**, and the bond joins the **anomeric carbon of
each**.
The anomeric carbon is the one derived from the carbonyl, so it is
**C-1 in glucose**, an **aldo**hexose whose carbonyl is at C-1
**C-2 in fructose**, a **keto**hexose whose carbonyl is at C-2
and the configurations are α for the glucose and β for the fructose. So the linkage runs
**C-1 of α-glucose to C-2 of β-fructose** ✓ — option (a).
The consequence of joining the two anomeric carbons is important: **neither** ring can open
any longer, so there is **no free aldehyde or ketone** anywhere in the molecule. That is why
sucrose is a **non-reducing** sugar, giving no reaction with Tollens' or Fehling's reagent,
and why it does not undergo mutarotation.
It is the only common disaccharide of which this is true, and the contrast identifies the
other options:
**(b)** C-1 of β-galactose to C-4 of glucose is **lactose**
**(c)** C-1 of α-glucose to C-4 of α-glucose is **maltose**
Both of those leave one anomeric carbon free, so both are reducing sugars.
∴ C-1 of α-glucose and C-2 of β-fructose.

The linkage joins C-1 of the glucose to C-2 of the fructose, tying up **both** anomeric
carbons, which is why sucrose is non-reducing.
∴ α-D-glucopyranose and β-D-fructofuranose.

glycosidic bond from C-1 of one to C-4 of the other.
So hydrolysis with dilute acid gives **two molecules of D-glucose**, and nothing else:
C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O --dil. HCl--> **2 C₆H₁₂O₆ (D-glucose)** ✓ — option (c)

apart:
**maltose** = glucose + glucose (α-1,4) — malt sugar, from the partial hydrolysis of starch
**lactose** = galactose + glucose (β-1,4) — option (d)'s galactose comes from here
**sucrose** = glucose + fructose (α-1,β-2) — option (a)
Since only **one** of maltose's two anomeric carbons is used in the link, the other is free,
the ring can open to expose an aldehyde, and maltose is therefore a **reducing** sugar that
shows mutarotation.
The α-1,4 bond is the same linkage found throughout **starch**, which is no accident: maltose
is literally a two-unit fragment of starch, produced when the enzyme amylase cuts the
polymer up. That is what happens in germinating barley, and why the sugar is named after
malt.

Glucose is an **aldo**hexose and fructose a **keto**hexose, so the test must distinguish an
aldose from a ketose.
**(a) Seliwanoff's test** ✓ — resorcinol with concentrated HCl. Under these conditions a
**ketose dehydrates much faster** than an aldose:
**fructose** gives a **cherry-red** colour within about **30 seconds**
**glucose** gives only a faint pink, and slowly, after several minutes
A clear difference in both colour and speed, so the two are distinguished ✓
The others fail because they respond to **any reducing sugar**, and both glucose and fructose
are reducing:
**(b) Benedict's test** ✗ — both give the red precipitate of Cu₂O
**(d) Fehling's test** ✗ — both give the red precipitate
Fructose reacts in these tests despite having no aldehyde group, because the alkaline
conditions **isomerise** it to glucose and mannose first. That isomerisation is exactly what
Seliwanoff's acidic conditions avoid, which is why it succeeds where the alkaline tests fail.
**(c) Barfoed's test** ✗ — this distinguishes **monosaccharides from disaccharides** by
reaction rate in a mildly acidic medium, not aldoses from ketoses. Both glucose and fructose
are monosaccharides and both react.
∴ Seliwanoff's test.
